title: Holidays and the calendar
topic: Israeli holidays; the months; giving holiday wishes
why: A practical culture lesson: the five holidays you'll come across in Israel, the months, the seasons and the greetings to know. It reuses the hitpa'el and the hif'il (to dress up, to light) in real-life situations.

{"lessons": ["

Months and seasons

In everyday life, Israelis use the same months as you, with almost the same names:

MonthHebrewPronunciation
Januaryיָנוּאָרyanuar
Februaryפֶבְּרוּאָרfebruar
Marchמֶרְץmerts
Aprilאַפְּרִילapril
Mayמַאיmai
Juneיוּנִיyuni
Julyיוּלִיyuli
Augustאוֹגוּסְטogust
Septemberסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּרseptember
Octoberאוֹקְטוֹבֶּרoktober
Novemberנוֹבֶמְבֶּרnovember
Decemberדֶּצֶמְבֶּרdetsember

\"In January\": בְּיָנוּאָר (be-yanuar). \"Which month?\": אֵיזֶה חֹדֶשׁ? (eize khodesh?).

The seasons: אָבִיב (aviv, spring, as in Tel Aviv, \"the hill of spring\"), קַיִץ (kayits, summer), סְתָו (stav, fall), חֹרֶף (khoref, winter).

The holidays, on the other hand, follow the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar: their date changes every year on the usual calendar, but each holiday stays in the same season. The Hebrew year begins in the fall, in September or October.

", "

The major holidays

HolidayWhenWhat people do
רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (rosh ha-shana)fallthe New Year: a family meal, people eat an apple dipped in honey, תַּפּוּחַ בִּדְבַשׁ (tapuakh bi-dvash), for a sweet year
חֲנֻכָּה (khanuka)winter, eight dayspeople light candles, נֵרוֹת (nerot), and eat doughnuts, סֻפְגָּנִיּוֹת (sufganiyot)
פּוּרִים (purim)end of winterkids and adults dress up in costumes; parties and parades in the streets
פֶּסַח (pesakh)spring, one weeka big family meal, people eat מַצָּה (matsa, flatbread); school vacation, many Israelis travel
יוֹם הָעַצְמָאוּת (yom ha-atsma'ut)springnational holiday: picnics and barbecues, מַנְגָּל (mangal), in the parks

\"On Passover,\" \"on Purim\": בְּפֶסַח, בְּפוּרִים; but before the חֲ of חֲנֻכָּה, בְּ is pronounced ba: בַּחֲנֻכָּה (ba-khanuka). \"During the holiday\": בַּחַג.

Two new verbs follow the binyanim of this unit: מִתְחַפֵּשׂ (hitpa'el, to dress up in a costume) and מַדְלִיק (hif'il, to light).

בְּפוּרִים הִיא מִתְחַפֶּשֶׂת לְמַלְכָּה.On Purim, she dresses up as a queen. [be-purim hi mitkhapeset le-malka]
בַּחֲנֻכָּה אֲנַחְנוּ מַדְלִיקִים נֵרוֹת.On Hanukkah, we light candles. [ba-khanuka anakhnu madlikim nerot]
", "

Wishing someone a happy holiday

GreetingPronunciationWhen
חַג שָׂמֵחַ!khag sameakhfor every holiday: \"happy holiday\"
שָׁנָה טוֹבָה!shana tovaon Rosh Hashanah: \"happy new year\"
שָׁנָה טוֹבָה וּמְתוּקָה!shana tova u-metuka\"a good and sweet year\"
חֲנֻכָּה שָׂמֵחַ! / פּוּרִים שָׂמֵחַ!khanuka sameakh / purim sameakhthe name of the holiday, then שָׂמֵחַ, always in the masculine, because you're thinking of חַג

To reply: גַּם לְךָ! (gam lekha, to a man) or גַּם לָךְ! (gam lakh, to a woman), \"you too.\" To several people: גַּם לָכֶם! (gam lakhem).

Practical tip: on the eve of a holiday, עֶרֶב חַג (erev khag), stores close early and the roads are packed. On the day itself of the major holidays (Rosh Hashanah, Passover), many shops and public transportation stop, just like on Shabbat. Do your shopping ahead of time!
